[PAPER_0006, relevance_score=0.282] The goal of the present study was to investigate whether and how target-related perceptual processes modulate the superimposition of target-based and distractor-based activations (and, with that, the observable conflict effects) in one of the most prominent conflict paradigms, the visual Simon task (e.g., Hoffmann et al., 2023; Hübner & Töbel, 2019; Luo & Proctor, 2018; Mittelstädt & Miller, 2018; Pratte et al., 2010; Simon, 1969; Wühr & Ansorge, 2005; reviews given by Hommel, 2011; Lu & Proctor, 1995).

[PAPER_0007, relevance_score=0.316] Specifically, we tested the predictions of fading activation accounts, which assume that changes in target-related processes affect Simon effects solely by altering the absolute contribution of fading distractor-based activation (e.g., Hommel, 1993a, 1994).

[PAPER_0027, relevance_score=0.293] A generally more salient stimulus may enhance the salience of the target's position relative to the reference, which, in turn, could also induce increased distractor-based activation. These possibilities are not mutually exclusive, and there may also be other potential explanations. In any case, the general point is that in these previous studies, there are several reasons to suspect that the target discriminability manipulation directly affected both target and distractor processing.

[PAPER_0033, relevance_score=0.284] In the General Discussion section, we delve into modified accounts while also considering exploratory modeling with a recent formal model of conflict tasks that considers the concept of fading activation (Ulrich et al., 2015).

[PAPER_0049, relevance_score=0.282] In other words, these comparisons based on linear fits (i.e., predicted Simon effects) offer a statistical test to directly investigate whether the Simon effect differs between the easy and hard conditions at the same absolute RT, as suggested by the visual inspection that the DPs did not overlap.

[PAPER_0065, relevance_score=0.341] Of course, these possibilities are not mutually exclusive and there may be other perspectives on how to explain the present pattern; however, as the goal of the present experiments was to test the general predictions of fading activation accounts with a novel perceptual target manipulation, we can only clearly interpret the results in terms of this account.

[PAPER_0067, relevance_score=0.282] between blocks) represent another novel finding. Previous studies have already suggested different effects of discriminability on mean Simon effects when a randomized versus blocked design is entertained, for example, when comparing Hommel (1993a) and Servant et al. (2014). However, the conflicting results of these aforementioned studies might also be explained by other methodological differences between the studies. However, in the present study, such an explanation can be excluded as the only difference between Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 was the manipulation of how perceptual difficulty varied (trialwise vs. blockwise).

[PAPER_0068, relevance_score=0.322] blockwise). Thus, a more methodological implication is that the decision to use a between-block versus within-block manipulation of a certain experimental factor might be more critical than one might expect (see also Christ, 1970). As mentioned before, the differences between experiments in the present study cannot be explained by potential sequential variations in difficulty in Experiment 1, as the pattern was largely consistent when only focusing on trials where target discriminability was repeated (as was obviously always the case in Experiment 2).

[PAPER_0069, relevance_score=0.289] Theoretically, it thus seems puzzling why a constant versus random fluctuation in target discriminability differentially influences the conflict effects in the Simon task. In hopes to shed some light on this issue, and to generally gain a deeper understanding of the effects from our experimental manipulations, we decided to complement our analysis by employing a model-based approach.

[PAPER_0079, relevance_score=0.285] random) may additionally modulate the impact of perceptual target discriminability on conflict processing.

Another interesting finding from the model-based analyses was that distractor-based activation reached its peak amplitude earlier in the easy condition compared to the hard condition in Experiment 1, whereas there was, if any, a slightly reversed effect in Experiment 2. While it seems unlikely that these differences can contribute to the opposing shifts of DPs across experiments, this pattern aligns well with the observed DP slopes.

[PAPER_0081, relevance_score=0.285] However, some studies suggest that more negative-going plot slopes and a corresponding earlier peak amplitude reflect a faster onset of inhibitory processes of distractor-based activation (e.g., Mittelstädt, Mackenzie, et al., 2023; Ridderinkhof, 2002). Thus, one speculative interpretation is that inhibition can begin earlier with easy compared to hard targets when discriminability is randomly varied in Experiment 1.

[PAPER_0100, relevance_score=0.310] Importantly, we found that the results of both experiments were highly consistent and comparable when analyzed solely based on the data of the initial 80 participants (or the initial 120 participants in Experiment 2). The sample size in the two experiments considered both practical constraints (e.g., participant availability) and empirical constraints (e.g., effect size in previous studies).

[PAPER_0101, relevance_score=0.298] With 80 participants, we would already have over 80% power to detect a significant effect for a potential shift between DPs (as measured via paired t test on predicted Simon effects, as in the present study) of at least dz = 0.32 at a significance level of α = .05 (two-sided). Moreover, the actual sample sizes of 115 participants (Experiment 1) and 121 participants (Experiment 2) allowed us to detect significant effects of at least dz = 0.27.

[PAPER_0035, relevance_score=0.260] Method

Participants

One hundred fifteen (115) participants (73 female) with a mean age of 43.2 (SD = 12.79), remained for analysis (an additional four participants were excluded because of ERs of 20% or higher).4 They were undergraduates from the University of Hagen and received course credit for participation.

[PAPER_0038, relevance_score=0.259] Task and Procedure

Overall, each participant was tested in 12 experimental blocks with each block including 56 randomly ordered trials, with seven presentations of each of the eight possible stimulus displays (i.e., 2 locations × 2 color majority × 2 discriminability). At the beginning of each trial, the fixation cross appeared on the screen for 500 ms and with its offset, the colored square appeared. The target remained on the screen until the participant responded, up to 2 s. After correct responses, the next trial started after the presentation of a blank screen for 500 ms.

[PAPER_0040, relevance_score=0.267] Data Preparation

For this and the subsequent experiment, we followed the same data preparation procedure as reported in Experiment 1 of Mittelstädt and Miller (2020).5 The first two blocks were considered practice and not analyzed. For both RT and error rate (ER) analyses, we excluded trials with RTs <200 ms as anticipations (0.03%) and trials without any response (0.34%). For RT analyses, we additionally excluded choice errors (3.87%).6

[PAPER_0103, relevance_score=0.236] 5

In this and the subsequent experiment, results were very similar when excluding only RTs <150 ms (as erroneously described in our preregistration). Additionally, the results were also very similar when posterror and posttimeout trials were excluded.

[PAPER_0131, relevance_score=0.342] Fitting Method

The DMC model was fitted to the individual data of the four conditions from each experiment with the R package DMCfun (Mackenzie & Dudschig, 2021). We fitted the model simultaneously to condition-specific errors and RT distributions. This was achieved by minimizing the root-mean-squared error (RMSE) between observed and predicted values, a technique used in previous studies (e.g., Ellinghaus et al., 2018; Mittelstädt, Miller, Leuthold, et al., 2022).

Statistical models To answer the question raised in the hypotheses section we will analyse the data on both mean and distributional level. First, we will report 2 x2 ANOVAs on mean RT and mean PE with the within-subject factors congruency (congruent vs. incongruent) and discriminability (easy vs. hard) to make the results more comparable to previous studies (e.g., Hommel, 1994).

[PREREG_0012, relevance_score=0.295] Second, we will compare the delta plots using the method introduced by Mittelstädt & Miller (2020). Specifically, we will compute delta plots using 9 percentiles (10%, 20%,...) separately for each participant within each discriminability condition. We will then summarize the delta plot for each participant and each condition with a linear regression model predicting the delta in each bin from the mean RT in that bin. To compare the time-courses of the RT delta plots, we will compute paired t-tests between the slopes of the easy vs.

[PREREG_0013, relevance_score=0.293] hard discriminability condition. To see whether changes in Simon effects can be explained entirely by time varying distractor-based activation, we will use the regression model for each condition to compute the predicted congruency effect at each participant's individual mean RT. Following this, a paired t-test will be conducted on the predicted congruency effects. Thus, this comparison allows to compare the Simon effect at a common RT and hence to control for response speed.

[PREREG_0015, relevance_score=0.334] For completeness we will also compute delta plots on percentage errors (PE). To better understand the effects of the discriminability manipulation on the Simon effect, we will also fit the observed (individual) behavioral data to the DMC model using the R-package DMC fun (Mackenzie & Dudschig, 2021) and compare the best-fitting parameters.

[PAPER_0003, relevance_score=0.248] In everyday life, individuals must often complete tasks involving both task-relevant information (targets) and task-irrelevant information (distractors). Cognitive psychologists have long aimed to understand the underlying processing mechanisms that allow individuals to transform sensory information into motor responses in such situations (Sanders, 1980; Welford, 1968).

One issue that arises when investigating the effect of manipulating perceptual processes on the mean Simon effect is the temporal characteristics of Simon effects across the reaction time distribution.

As mentioned before, the differences between experiments in the present study cannot be explained by potential sequential variations in difficulty in Experiment 1, as the pattern was largely consistent when only focusing on trials where target discriminability was repeated (as was obviously always the case in Experiment 2).

[PAPER_0069, relevance_score=0.257] Theoretically, it thus seems puzzling why a constant versus random fluctuation in target discriminability differentially influences the conflict effects in the Simon task. [PAPER_0089, relevance_score=0.335] Possible Extensions to Other Processing Manipulations

The present approach of combining DP and diffusion model analyses with experimental manipulations of processing characteristics (in this case, perceptual target processing) can also be applied in other contexts (e.g., different conflict tasks) to better understand the underlying mechanisms of conflict processing. For example, presenting targets in a Simon task as far versus near might influence the strength of distractor-based activation (i.e., larger when targets are far than when they are near, as location differences are more salient and require larger attentional shifts).

[PAPER_0090, relevance_score=0.258] However, looking only at mean RT makes it difficult to understand the effects because task processing is also slower when targets are far compared to when they are near (Hommel, 1993a). Furthermore, more fine-grained modeling and/or DP analyses may also help to better understand why such a manipulation produces different effects on mean Simon effects in a within-block versus between-block manipulation; for some discussion, see Hommel (1993a).

[PAPER_0092, relevance_score=0.252] In these cases, DP and/or diffusion model analyses are also helpful as they show that the effects of processing speed can sometimes be solely explained by the time course of distractor-based activation (e.g., Mittelstädt, Miller, Leuthold, et al., 2022), but sometimes not (e.g., Kelber, Gierlich, et al., 2023).
